items.title: From Advice to Emergencies: Public Perceptions of AI Support in Social Media Service Requests
items.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in public service delivery raises critical questions about the types of citizen requests that warrant attention and the extent to which the public trusts AI compared to human responders. This study examines safety and service related requests expressed on social media and explores public perceptions of AI and human responses to such requests. Using a mixed methods design, the study combines a qualitative content analysis of social media posts with semi-structured interviews conducted with members of the general public. The findings identify multiple categories of serviceable requests, including preventive and reassurance seeking safety concerns, guidance and escalation needs, and emergency preparedness and procedural guidance. These requests reflect how individuals use social media to seek advice, reassurance, and direction when formal public service channels are perceived as unclear, slow, or inaccessible. Interview findings further reveal that trust in AI is highly situational. Participants generally viewed AI as acceptable for low stakes, informational, and time sensitive situations, where rapid access to answers was prioritized. However, AI was largely rejected for high risk, medical, or life-threatening scenarios, where concerns about reliability, authority, and accountability were prominent. Participants consistently distinguished between the availability of AI generated responses and their perceived trustworthiness.

items.title: From AI Detection to AI Literacy-Rethinking Academic Integrity in Higher Education
items.abstract: The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has raised concerns about academic integrity, institutional policies, and the reliability of AI detection tools. This paper examines the limitations of detection-based enforcement and argues for an approach centered on AI literacy, ethical responsibility, and critical thinking. Drawing on published studies, institutional surveys, and research findings, it discusses the widespread adoption of AI among students and educators, the risk of false accusations from detection systems, inconsistent university policies, and gaps in faculty preparedness. Particular attention is given to the challenges faced by non-native English speakers and students with limited access to digital resources. The discussion emphasizes the need to teach students how to verify AI-generated information, acknowledge AI assistance, recognize bias, and make responsible academic decisions. It also highlights the importance of faculty training, clear institutional guidelines, and assessment practices that encourage independent reasoning. items.title: From Articulation to Enforcement: District Governance of Generative AI Under Policy Ambiguity in Chicago Public Schools
items.abstract: Districts must govern generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in K–12 education without binding federal or state mandates. This study examines how Chicago Public Schools (CPS) publicly articulated a district-level GenAI governance model during 2023 to 2025, through document analysis and policy tracing. Analysis is guided by equity-anchored implementation, a construct linking implementation theory and data justice: equity commitments endure in proportion to the degree and focus of their institutional embedding. CPS articulated flexible guidance, human oversight, vendor accountability, and prohibitions on high-risk uses, alongside an articulation-enforcement gap: commitments are detailed, but monitoring, enforcement, and differentiated supports are less documented. A bounded comparison with New York City, Philadelphia, and Miami-Dade shows that institutional anchors narrow gaps only in domains they directly govern. It reframes policy ambiguity as a condition for governance articulation, distinguishes equity as harm prevention from capacity distribution, and concludes that AI governance should be judged by institutional capacity, not policy sophistication.

items.title: From Beijing to Brussels: pathways to the integration of gender in research and development (IGIRD)
items.abstract: Abstract This article offers a first consolidated historical account of the institutionalisation of the Integration of Gender in Research and Development (IGiRD). We use IGiRD as an analytical umbrella term for policies, instruments and research practices that integrate sex and gender analysis into the content, design, evaluation and governance of research and development. The article centres on how sex and gender analysis became institutionally anchored as a question of research quality, responsibility and societal relevance, while treating gender representation in research careers as a related but distinct issue. Drawing on an event-based historical reconstruction of 186 policy and institutional events from 1957 to 2024, the article traces how IGiRD developed across four partially overlapping pathways: gender equality and anti-discrimination frameworks, women’s advancement in science and technology, health and medical research, and broader integration of sex and gender analysis across research fields and governance structures. Comparing the EU, US, Canada and South Korea, the analysis shows that IGiRD has not followed a single linear trajectory. The EU pathway is distinctive because gender mainstreaming became layered onto supranational research funding and evaluation structures, while North America demonstrates strong sectoral anchoring in health and biomedical research, and South Korea illustrates rapid formal-legal anchoring with incomplete operational embedding. The article contributes to historical-institutionalist science policy research by conceptualising IGiRD institutionalisation as layered, recursive and politically reversible. Formal anchoring in laws, strategies or funding rules matters, but durable change depends on operational embedding through review expertise, guidance, training, monitoring and feedback mechanisms, and on substantive methodological integration in research practice. This perspective clarifies why IGiRD can be stabilised, narrowed or reactivated under changing political conditions and offers policy implications for strengthening gender-sensitive R&I in emerging fields such as artificial intelligence.

items.title: From benchmark to user: an end-to-end evaluation audit of an AI-based oral health screening prototype
items.abstract: Background Artificial intelligence (AI) for oral screening is usually judged by aggregate detection metrics on public benchmarks whose partitions, labels, and relevance to users are rarely checked. Methods We audited a prototype combining a YOLOv8m detector for six conditions (1,500 test images), a DenseNet169 histopathology network, and a ResNet18 router. Under a pre-specified plan, we measured duplication across partitions, tested removal of duplicated test images against 10,000 matched controls, compared duplicated copies' labels and predictions, compared the library versions, and ran every test image through the application pipeline. Results Near-duplicates of training images accounted for 17.3% of test and 17.1% of validation images (lower bounds). Removing duplicated test images changed mean average precision (mAP)@0.5 by +0.001 (95% confidence interval [CI] −0.012 to +0.014). Only 22% of duplicated photographs had identical labels on both copies; exploratory analysis suggested memorization of training labels in orientations seen in training. A library update moved mAP@0.5:0.95 by −0.012 with identical predictions. The router rejected 23% of in-domain photographs and 51% of photographs with ulcers, so ulcer sensitivity per image was 0.36 despite the highest benchmark recall (0.91). A class-mapping defect, still live in a public demonstration in September 2026, gave the wrong name to 73% of findings. The histopathology classifier classified every image as positive; its label was not a diagnosis. Conclusion Duplication compromised the benchmark's independence without detectably changing aggregate mAP; the defects that changed what was reported or displayed lay in the labels, evaluation software, and pipeline. Evaluations should verify partitions and labels, pin the library, and test deployed systems end to end.

items.title: From Bookkeeper to Sustainability Strategist: A Qualitative Exploration of the Evolving Role of the Accountant in the Era of AI, Sustainability and Digital Taxation in Nigeria
items.abstract: Artificial Intelligence, sustainability reporting under IFRS S1 and S2, and digital tax administration are reshaping the accounting profession in Nigeria, yet there is little qualitative evidence on how the accountant’s role has changed or what competencies it now demands. This study explored the evolving role of the accountant in Nigeria through the lived experiences of senior practitioners. A qualitative phenomenological design was adopted. Twenty-five senior accountants with at least 15 years of post-qualification experience in Lagos, Abuja and Port Harcourt were purposively selected: 5 ICAN Fellows/Professors, 6 Big 4 and mid-tier audit partners, 8 industry CFOs and 6 public sector directors. Semi-structured interviews were conducted between January and May 2025, with saturation reached at the 21st interview. Data were analysed thematically using the Braun and Clarke framework with NVivo 12, collapsing 78 codes into four themes. A four-stage evolution model emerged: Bookkeeper (1990–2005), Financial Reporter (2006–2015), Digital Analyst (2016–2023) and Sustainability and AI Strategist (2024–date). Five future-ready competency domains were identified (technical accounting, taxation, audit and assurance, sustainability reporting, and soft and ethical skills), each cited by 80%–96% of participants. The main barriers were curriculum obsolescence (88%), technophobia (72%), cost and infrastructure (68%), absence of Nigerian emission factors (64%) and regulatory uncertainty (56%). A five-pillar framework spanning regulators, professional bodies, universities, corporate organisations and individual accountants is proposed to make Nigerian accountants future-ready and globally competitive.

items.title: From Cheating to Coaching: How Chemistry Syllabi Frame Academic Integrity in the Age of Generative AI
items.abstract: Abstract Generative artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly changing expectations for academic integrity in higher education, yet it remains unclear how institutional AI governance is translated into course-level guidance. This study examines how academic integrity and generative AI are framed in chemistry course documents and institutional policy documents. Using a hybrid inductive–deductive qualitative document analysis, I analyzed 18 publicly available chemistry course documents and 17 institutional policy documents from nine institutions across four countries. The analysis identified five higher-order themes in chemistry course documents: consequence-focused framing of academic integrity; academic integrity framed primarily as student responsibility; boilerplate policy language dominating over contextualized integrity guidance; generative AI addressed through silence, ambiguity, or prohibition; and faculty guidance and prevention rarely being explicit. A direct comparison revealed a substantial governance gap: 15 of 17 institutional policy documents (88.2%) explicitly mentioned generative AI, compared with only 2 of 18 chemistry course documents (11.1%). Institutional policies also more frequently addressed faculty guidance, research guidance, and AI governance than course documents. These findings suggest that institutional AI governance is developing more rapidly than its translation into chemistry course-level practice. Although policies and syllabi will continue to evolve as generative AI changes, the documented governance gap provides a baseline for examining how institution-level guidance is translated into instructional practice over time. The study concludes by proposing a coaching-oriented approach that shifts syllabus guidance from primarily punitive restrictions toward transparent, ethical, and pedagogically purposeful AI use.

items.title: From Coding Assistants to Self-Healing Terminals: NeuraOS A Critical Review of AI-Driven Autonomous Command Execution and Error Recovery on Linux Systems
items.abstract: The Linux command-line interface continues to serve as the primary control surface for software development, systems administration, and cloud operations, yet it executes instructions syntactically, without semantic awareness of user intent and without built-in mechanisms for diagnosing or repairing runtime failures. Over roughly the last decade, three largely distinct research communities have each addressed part of this problem: large language model (LLM)-based coding assistants embedded in integrated development environments (IDEs), natural-language-to-command translation systems that lower the barrier to shell usage, and operating-systems research on self-healing and autonomic computing that targets distributed and cloud infrastructure rather than the interactive terminal. This paper presents a structured, critical review of these three strands, together with the log-based anomaly-detection and AIOps literature that supplies much of the diagnostic machinery such systems would require. Literature was retained where it addressed semantic command interpretation, real-time or near-real-time failure diagnosis, autonomous or semi-autonomous recovery, or persistence of prior failure-resolution experience. The reviewed work is organized along four analytical dimensions — runtime integration, autonomy level, diagnostic depth, and knowledge retention — and compared qualitatively across these dimensions. The synthesis shows that autonomy and diagnostic sophistication increase substantially when moving from IDE assistants toward self-healing infrastructure research, but this increase is accompanied by a shift away from the single-operator, single-machine terminal context, and that no reviewed system combines real-time in-terminal diagnosis, multi-pathway recovery, and durable per-machine experiential learning while remaining confined to user space. The review further discusses recurring safety and governance themes — confidence-gated autonomy, privilege-aware execution, and explanation-first human oversight — that constrain the design space for any terminal-level orchestration layer, and it identifies four concrete research gaps together with a near-, mid-, and long-term research roadmap. The review does not claim that any single technology described is either novel or previously unstudied in isolation; its contribution is the cross-domain synthesis and the identification of the specific combination of properties that remains unaddressed.

items.title: From Culturally Grounded Virtual Games to Real-World Destination Engagement: Flow, Cultural Identity and Behavioral Intention Conversion
items.abstract: Culturally embedded virtual games increasingly shape digital design, cultural communication, and place experience, yet how immersion translates into real-world engagement remains unclear. Drawing on the cognition–affect–conation model and flow theory, this study analyzes survey data from 458 young players. Presence, perceived realism, and curiosity significantly enhance emotional interaction and flow, while challenge improves flow but not emotional interaction. Flow mediates the relationship between virtual cultural experience and intention to visit real-world places; emotional interaction has no direct effect. Cultural identity strengthens the flow–participation relationship, highlighting its role in converting virtual immersion into cultural engagement. Culturally grounded games therefore function as destination pre-experience and cultural design platforms, through which digital scenes, cultural symbols, and interaction shape players’ imagination, identification, and willingness to participate in real-world cultural spaces. Findings inform game design, heritage communication, and place-experience design.

items.title: From goal framing to participation experience: a cognitive-affective process perspective on mass participation sport events
items.abstract: Purpose This study opens the “psychological black box” of participation experiences in mass participation sport events (MPSEs) by examining how goal frames are associated with experiential outcomes through cognitive engagement and psychological empowerment. Drawing on goal-framing theory and the cognitive-affective processing system (CAPS), it proposes a process model linking goal frames to participation experiences, with social connectedness as a boundary condition. Design/methodology/approach A quantitative survey was conducted with participants in Taiwan who had engaged in non-elite sport events within the past year (N = 405). Data were analyzed using PLS-SEM with bootstrapping, employing established scales to measure goal framing, cognitive engagement, psychological empowerment, event enjoyment, subjective vitality, and social connectedness. Findings All three goal frames were positively associated with cognitive engagement and psychological empowerment. Cognitive engagement was positively associated with both event enjoyment and subjective vitality, whereas psychological empowerment was positively associated with subjective vitality but not event enjoyment. Social connectedness significantly moderated the relationship between psychological empowerment and subjective vitality, while the other moderation effects were not statistically significant. The indirect effects further revealed two distinct pathways, with cognitive engagement operating across both experiential outcomes and psychological empowerment being associated with subjective vitality. Originality/value This study advances a process-based perspective by integrating goal-framing theory with CAPS to explain how goal frames are associated with experiential outcomes through cognitive engagement and psychological empowerment. It demonstrates that social connectedness functions as a selective rather than universal boundary condition.

items.title: From Goals to Results: An Analytical Perspective on Three Global Challenges Through the Lens of Project Management
items.abstract: This independent analytical paper examines three major global challenges: biodiversity protection, the future of work in the age of artificial intelligence, and global supply chain resilience. Through the lens of project management, the paper explores the gap between global commitments and effective implementation, the unequal distribution of opportunities and resources, and the importance of accountability, education, and human empowerment. It argues that meaningful progress should be measured not only by stated goals, technological advances, or economic indicators, but also by tangible and lasting improvements in people's lives and opportunities. The paper reflects the author's personal perspective and applies project management principles to the analysis of complex global challenges.

items.title: From Hazard Maps to Decision Intelligence: A Critical Review of GIS, Remote Sensing and GeoAI for Disaster Risk Management and Engineering Resilience
items.abstract: Disaster risk is inherently spatial, yet geographic information systems (GIS) are still frequently used to end analysis at a classified hazard map rather than to support an engineering or operational decision. This critical review traces how GIS, integrated with remote sensing (RS), multi-criteria decision analysis (MCDA), Web-GIS and geospatial artificial intelligence (GeoAI), has evolved across the disaster management cycle, and evaluates whether the resulting products are validated, uncertainty-aware and usable in civil-engineering practice. Twenty foundational studies (1992–2017) covering general emergency management, floods, earthquakes, landslides, cyclones and coastal hazards, drought and forest fire are appraised against a structured set of dimensions and are updated with recent systematic reviews of Web-GIS, AI/ML-enabled GIS, drone-based hazard sensing and AI-based landslide analysis. Four analytical families (knowledge-driven, data-driven, simulation-based and integrated Web-GIS/GeoAI) are compared. Knowledge-driven methods such as AHP and weighted overlay remain valuable where event inventories are scarce but are sensitive to expert-assigned weights; statistical and machine-learning models can improve prediction but are vulnerable to spatial leakage, non-representative inventories and limited interpretability; operational Web-GIS and GeoAI systems are advancing quickly but are rarely validated against independent events or evaluated by their effect on decisions. The most persistent gap is the translation of hazard classes into engineering quantities such as flood depth and velocity, design ground motion, slope safety factors, damage states and lifeline reliability. The review proposes (i) an eight-stage data-to-decision framework linking GIS, RS, GeoAI and engineering analysis, (ii) a minimum reporting and validation checklist for GIS-based hazard studies, and (iii) a prioritised research agenda covering multi-hazard modelling, near-real-time Web-GIS, uncertainty-aware GeoAI, digital twins, BIM–GIS integration and decision-centric validation.

items.title: From Legal Pads to Artificial Intelligence: How Technology Has Changed the Work of the Preacher—and What Must Never Change
items.abstract: Description Artificial intelligence is changing how people research, write, and communicate, raising important questions for the church and the work of the preacher. How can pastors benefit from emerging technologies without surrendering the personal study, prayer, theological judgment, and spiritual responsibility essential to faithful preaching? In From Legal Pads to Artificial Intelligence: How Technology Has Changed the Work of the Preacher—and What Must Never Change, Brent Madaris, D.Min., examines the relationship between technological assistance and the preacher’s personal responsibility in sermon preparation. Drawing on pastoral ministry, theological study, and professional experience in healthcare, the author considers both the potential benefits and the limitations of artificial intelligence in vocational ministry. The essay distinguishes between using AI as a tool for research, organization, and refinement and allowing it to substitute for the preacher’s own biblical study, spiritual reflection, theological discernment, and pastoral judgment. It also considers how lessons from the responsible use of AI in clinical practice may inform discussions about its use in ministry. Rather than offering an unqualified endorsement or rejection of artificial intelligence, this work argues for thoughtful and responsible engagement with emerging technology while maintaining the convictions and practices that must remain central to Christian preaching. AI may assist in preparing a sermon, but it cannot prepare the preacher. This essay is intended for pastors, ministry leaders, theological educators, students, and others interested in preaching, Christian ministry, theological reflection, and the ethical use of artificial intelligence. Keywords: Artificial intelligence; sermon preparation; preaching; pastoral ministry; Christian ministry; theological education; Christian ethics; technology and religion; responsible AI use.

items.title: From Personalization to Manipulation: A Systematic Review of Ethical Issues of AI and its Impact on Young Users Through Social Media
items.abstract: This systematic review examines how artificial intelligence (AI) shapes the digital experiences of young users through social media reels and personalized content. The study focuses on the ethical dimensions of these developments, addressing concerns such as algorithmic bias, data privacy, exposure to potentially harmful content, and the broader psychological effects on adolescents. This paper evaluates current literature to uncover the ethical tensions between personalization and manipulation. Following the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines, this review systematically analysed 42 peer-reviewed articles and industry reports published between 2015 and 2024. The analysis highlights how AI's profit-driven logic reinforces compulsive behaviours, body image concerns, and social comparison among adolescents. Such effects are particularly pronounced among adolescents, who are in a critical stage of identity formation and are more vulnerable to the psychological consequences of digital exposure. To address these challenges, the paper proposes a multi-stakeholder ethical framework designed to promote algorithmic transparency, empower young users through digital literacy, and enhance regulatory accountability. This framework emphasizes the shared responsibility of technology companies, policymakers, educators, and guardians in mitigating the adverse impacts of AI-driven personalization. The review's insights hold significant relevance for those seeking to balance innovation with ethical safeguards in the evolving landscape of youth, technology, and social media.

items.title: From Prediction to Interaction: A Behavioral Informatics Framework for AI in Preventive Health
items.abstract: Abstract In this viewpoint, we present our perspective—informed by published evidence and by our own work on AI-driven digital health systems—on why AI has had limited real-world impact in preventive health and how it should be redesigned. Most AI systems in health care are built as episodic prediction tools, whereas preventive care depends on sustained behavioral change; the consequences are visible in consistently high attrition and low long-term adherence across digital health interventions. The aim of this viewpoint is to argue that this failure is structural rather than incremental and to propose an integrated, interaction-centric alternative. We advance 3 key messages. First, the limited impact of AI in preventive health reflects a structural misalignment between episodic, prediction-centric system design and the longitudinal dynamics of health behavior. Second, addressing this misalignment requires treating continuous interaction as the primary unit of design, which we articulate through a behavioral informatics framework integrating 6 interdependent layers: data, knowledge, reasoning, interaction, behavior, and governance. The contribution of this framework is explicitly integrative: it synthesizes previously separate strands, including just-in-time adaptive interventions, behavioral intervention technologies, and human-AI interaction research, into a single system-level account. Third, evaluation must shift from predictive accuracy and short-term engagement toward measurable behavioral trajectories and longitudinal outcomes, with explicit attention to feasibility and to conditions under which simpler, non-AI interventions remain preferable. This viewpoint is addressed to digital health researchers and AI developers, behavioral scientists, clinicians involved in preventive care, and policymakers responsible for governing continuously interacting AI systems.

items.title: From publication to practice: Building a global home for interventional epidemiology and public health
items.abstract: Editorial Taking up the role of Managing Editor of the Journal of Interventional Epidemiology and Public Health (JIEPH) is both a privilege and a call to stewardship. I take over from Dr Sheba Nakacubo Gitta, who served as JIEPH’s Managing Editor until December 2025. My experience within the Journal’s editorial leadership, first as Deputy Managing Editor from October 2024 to December 2025 and then as Acting Managing Editor from January to September 2026, taught me firsthand how much this Journal owes to the people around it. It is with that appreciation that I approach this first editorial in my new role. JIEPH was launched in November 2018 in Maputo, Mozambique, during the 7th AFENET Scientific Conference, as an online, open-access, peer-reviewed scientific journal published by the African Field Epidemiology Network (AFENET) [1]. It has since grown into an open-access journal that publishes contextually relevant evidence from Africa and beyond, without charging article processing or submission fees and letting authors retain copyright through a Creative Commons Attribution license [2]. These foundations, laid by the journal’s founders, publishers, previous and current editorial leaders, authors, reviewers, readers and institutional partners, are what we build on today. Where we stand Publication output has grown substantially. In 2024, JIEPH published 77 articles: 57 regular articles, 10 in the Rwanda Field Epidemiology Training Programme supplement, and 10 in the first volume of the 8th AFENET Scientific Conference supplement [3]. In 2025, it published 149 articles: 105 regular articles and 44 supplement articles covering Togo FETP, Sierra Leone FETP and Volume 2 of the eighth AFENET Scientific Conference supplement [3]. As of mid-October 2026, Volume 9 carries 170 regular articles and 34 supplement articles, a combined total of 204. The journal has cumulatively published 15 supplements and eight conference proceedings [4]. Recent supplements and proceedings include contributions from the Guinea and Uganda Field Epidemiology Training Programmes, the 2nd ECOWAS Lassa fever regional conference, and AFENET @20 commemorative special issues [3]. These figures demonstrate increased publishing activity; the next challenge is to translate that growth into sustained scientific quality and evidence use. JIEPH’s visibility has grown alongside its publication output. The journal was added to the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) in April 2025 [2]. JIEPH’s indexing and abstracting coverage includes Scopus, CABI Global Health and CAB Abstracts; it also has a SCImago journal profile and is discoverable through EBSCOhost [5,6]. My ambition for JIEPH’s next stage is to build a global home for interventional epidemiology and public health, rooted in Africa’s field epidemiology community. Researchers and practitioners anywhere should be able to turn to the journal for rigorous, practice-relevant evidence on outbreaks, surveillance, public health programmes and population health. The central question is therefore no longer simply how much we can publish, but how we strengthen the quality, visibility, influence, inclusiveness and sustainability of what we publish, and how that evidence moves into practice. Four connected priorities will guide this phase: expanding indexation and discoverability, improving scientific and public health impact, nurturing the next generation of scientists, and building a sustainable journal. Becoming a global home is the ambition that connects these priorities, rather than a separate objective. Scientific quality, research integrity, editorial independence and responsible publishing will underpin them all. Expanding global visibility and discoverability Researchers, public health institutions and programmes in Africa and around the world continue to generate valuable evidence through outbreak investigations, surveillance, epidemiological studies, laboratory systems, programme implementation and community interventions. Publishing that evidence is not enough if researchers, practitioners, policymakers and communities, in any country, find it hard to discover and use. JIEPH is indexed in the Directory of Open Access Journals (DOAJ) and African Journals Online (AJOL). Its content and metadata are also discoverable through Google Scholar, OpenAlex, Scilit and OpenAIRE, with Crossref supporting metadata dissemination [5]. Sustaining and extending this visibility is the next task. Respondents to the 2026 half-year post-publication author survey identified broader coverage in databases such as PubMed and Web of Science as an important priority [7]. Inclusion in indexing services is decided by external bodies and cannot be secured by aspiration alone. JIEPH will therefore concentrate on what lies within its control: consistently meeting the scientific, editorial, ethical, technical and publishing standards that wider indexation requires, including complete article metadata and timely publication. Our aim is not merely to enter more databases but to be a journal whose quality, consistency, transparency and reliability merit sustained inclusion. Moving from publication to practice Authors see JIEPH as a natural home for field-based public health work. In a post-publication survey conducted between 26 June and 1 July 2026, 25 authors from 15 countries across West, East, Central and Southern Africa reported a mean overall satisfaction of 8.9 out of 10. The mean likelihood of recommending JIEPH was 9.4 out of 10 and of submitting again 9.3 out of 10. Importantly, 88% said that publishing in JIEPH had enhanced the visibility of their work [7]. That reach already extends beyond the continent. Recent articles include a molecular surveillance study from a state public health laboratory in Mexico [8], and a commentary from the World Health Organization’s Health Emergencies Programme in Geneva, Switzerland, on our Sierra Leone mpox cohort study, which presents that experience as a model for preparedness in Africa and globally [9]. A review of mobile public health emergency operations centres by an author based in the United States with a co-author at Africa CDC, has drawn nearly 9,000 views on the journal website [10]. Authors in India have published a study of carbonated beverage knowledge and practice among medical students in Kerala [11], and authors in Pakistan a letter on over-the-counter medicine and antibiotic misuse [12], while authors from Yemen’s Field Epidemiology Training Program and national AFP surveillance programme have reported ten years of acute flaccid paralysis surveillance data from Sana’a [13]. Together these show a journal whose subjects extend from outbreak response to non-communicable diseases and antimicrobial resistance. These findings encourage us, and they also challenge us to define impact more ambitiously. Readership, citation and inclusion in evidence syntheses matter, but bibliometrics alone cannot capture a public health journal’s contribution. For JIEPH, the larger question is whether evidence strengthens surveillance, improves outbreak preparedness and response, informs programmes and policy, guides resource allocation, supports teaching and training, and ultimately contributes to better population health, in Africa and wherever the work is used. The proposed public health emergency management curriculum published in the journal illustrates the kind of practice-oriented contribution we seek [14]. Our immediate contribution will be to encourage submissions that pair scientific rigour with clear relevance to public health action. We will ask authors, reviewers and editors to make three points explicit: what was found, why it matters, and how it could inform practice. Lessons from interventional epidemiology in African settings, including outbreak response under resource constraints, are relevant to health systems everywhere, and we want them to travel. We therefore need to ask not only how often articles are cited, but whether they are read, discussed, taught, translated into programmes and used in decisions. These steps can support evidence use; demonstrating changes in programmes, policy or population health will require evidence beyond publication metrics. Publication should be the beginning of scientific engagement, not its end. Nurturing the next generation of scientists Capacity development has long been part of JIEPH’s identity. Since 2021, the journal has hosted quarterly scientific-writing webinars and supported podcasts, workshops, French-language access and resources for researchers and authors [15]. The author survey provides encouraging feedback on editorial experience: professionalism of editorial communication and fairness of peer review each received a 96% positive rating, and respondents reported that reviewers helped improve the methodology, clarity and discussion of their manuscript [7]. These findings support the value of constructive editorial engagement and suggest that the developmental approach is reaching its intended audience. Our ambition is therefore twofold: to provide a platform for excellent science from Africa and the world, and to help develop the people who produce, review, communicate and use that science. Developing scientific capacity begins with making standards explicit, applying them consistently, and giving feedback that strengthens authors’ methods, reporting and interpretation. It also requires a growing community of skilled reviewers, editors, statistical advisers and publication professionals from Africa and across the world. Reviewer development, mentorship and early-career editorial opportunities can help build that community. Continuing education can strengthen the use of appropriate reporting guidelines, responsible artificial intelligence and publication ethics, alongside scientific writing. items.title: From sensing to clinical translation: advances and challenges in wearable cuffless blood pressure monitoring
items.abstract: Purpose This paper aims to systematically synthesize state-of-the-art advancements in wearable cuffless blood pressure (BP) monitoring technologies, critically examining the sensing hardware, estimation algorithms and calibration strategies and identifying the core barriers that impede the translation from laboratory prototypes to clinically reliable cardiovascular monitoring systems. Design/methodology/approach This paper adopts a comprehensive literature review approach, systematically analyzing emerging sensing modalities – including optoelectronic (PPG), mechanoelectric (triboelectric, piezoelectric, piezoresistive), ultrasonic and multimodal fusion systems – alongside the evolutionary trajectory of BP estimation techniques, from mechanism-driven models (PTT/PWV) through data-driven deep learning to the emerging physics-informed artificial intelligence paradigm. Clinical validation frameworks and calibration strategies are also critically assessed. Findings The review reveals that while significant progress has been made in sensor sensitivity, signal processing and algorithmic accuracy, several critical barriers persist before widespread clinical adoption. These include motion-induced signal degradation, limited cross-population generalizability of algorithms, the absence of standardized validation protocols for cuffless devices and calibration drift over time. Physics-informed AI emerges as a promising paradigm for improving robustness, interpretability and generalization by embedding hemodynamic constraints into data-driven models. Research limitations/implications As a review paper, the findings are based on published literature rather than original experimental data. Future research should focus on adaptive calibration frameworks, rigorous multi-scenario validation aligned with ESH 2023 recommendations and hardware-software co-design approaches. Practical implications The review provides actionable guidance for researchers, clinicians, and device developers by identifying key technological bottlenecks and outlining future directions, including endogenous autonomous calibration benchmarks and multimodal sensing integration, to accelerate the development of clinically viable wearable BP monitoring systems. Originality/value This paper uniquely bridges the gap between sensing hardware and clinical requirements by providing an integrated analysis across the full technology chain – from sensors to algorithms to clinical translation. It highlights physics-informed AI as a critical emerging direction and proposes a forward-looking framework for all-scenario adaptive dynamic calibration, offering a comprehensive roadmap for the field.

items.abstract: Purpose: Healthcare-associated infections (HAIs) remain a major clinical and economic burden, and early detection of transmission clusters is essential for timely intervention. Whole-genome sequencing (WGS) is the reference standard for outbreak confirmation, but its cost, turnaround time, and operational requirements limit its use as an always-on first-line surveillance tool. Because matrix-assisted laser desorption/ionization time-of-flight mass spectrometry (MALDI-TOF MS) spectra are already generated during routine species identification, they may provide a rapid triage layer before confirmatory sequencing. Methods: We synthesize current evidence for artificial intelligence (AI)-based MALDI-TOF MS analysis in within-species typing, strain relatedness inference, and outbreak-oriented surveillance. We organize the literature into three methodological pathways: peak-centric biomarker typing, supervised subtype classification, and representation learning. Results: The available evidence indicates that AI-based models can extract within-species signals from MALDI-TOF MS spectra that are relevant to typing and outbreak surveillance, but performance remains context-dependent. Peak-based approaches offer interpretability but are vulnerable to spectral instability and limited portability. Supervised classifiers can perform well for narrow predefined targets, but depend on fixed label spaces and may degrade when local epidemiology changes. Representation-learning approaches are less clinically validated for typing, but may offer the most scalable route toward adaptable, similarity-based early-warning systems. Conclusions: MALDI-TOF MS should not be viewed as a replacement for WGS, but as a locally calibrated decision-support tool that prioritizes suspicious isolates for sequencing and infection prevention and control (IPC) review, similar to a screening tool. Future studies should move beyond retrospective accuracy estimates and evaluate prospective clinical utility, including time gained, sequencing saved, false-alert burden, portability to new laboratories, and performance after minimal local calibration.

items.title: From task-specific networks to foundation models in diabetes care: a critical review of opportunities, evaluation gaps, and safety frontiers
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence in diabetes care has historically relied on task-specific supervised learning, such as bespoke networks for retinopathy grading, kidney disease prediction, and glucose forecasting. The emergence of foundation models (FMs: large models pretrained on broad data, typically with self-supervision, and adapted to many downstream tasks) is displacing this paradigm across diabetes-relevant modalities: ophthalmic models such as RETFound, pretrained on 1.6 million retinal photographs, have been reported to outperform task-specific networks on retinopathy grading and systemic disease prediction, especially when labeled data are scarce; transformer-based time-series models are replacing long short-term memory (LSTM) pipelines for continuous glucose monitoring (CGM) forecasting; clinical large language models (LLMs) such as Med-PaLM and GPT-4 attain expert-level scores on medical question-answering benchmarks; and generative models supply synthetic CGM and electronic health record (EHR) data. This review provides a critical, modality-organized synthesis of this transition. We (i) formalize a three-era taxonomy: rule-based risk scores (era I), task-specific deep learning (era II, 2016–2020), and foundation models (era III, from 2021), and map the diabetes literature onto it; (ii) survey foundation-model architectures, pretraining objectives, and adaptation strategies across retinal imaging, CGM, longitudinal EHR, and multimodal data; (iii) expose an evaluation crisis: benchmark contamination of LLM medical evaluations, a near-universal absence in the literature we reviewed of external and prospective validation for retinal and CGM foundation models, miscalibration under dataset shift, and, to our knowledge and within the reviewed literature (January 2016–December 2025; negative findings are time-sensitive), the absence of any randomized evaluation of a foundation model in a diabetes workflow; and (iv) analyze safety risks: hallucinated insulin-dosing advice, automation bias, inherited algorithmic inequity, and privacy exposure during adaptation. We conclude that the decisive open problem is no longer representation learning but grounded, calibrated, causally informed deployment, requiring contamination-resistant evaluation, prospective trials, and hybrid architectures coupling foundation-model representations with treatment-effect estimation.

items.title: From text-to-image to text-to-video: the reconfiguration of prompting practice in human-AI co-creation in 2022–2025
items.abstract: Introduction The movement of generative artificial intelligence from still-image to moving-image creation has reshaped the symbolic mechanism of human-AI co-creation. Methods This comparative observational study asks how prompt expression changes when the output shifts from static images to moving images, comparing two large-scale public prompt corpora under one neural topic-modeling protocol that combines lexical analysis of style, quality, technical, motion, camera, and format vocabulary with manual family coding and validity checks, and adds an exploratory user-focused topic structure. Results Video prompts weaken the style, quality, and technical decoration characteristic of image prompts and instead organize meaning around action, scene, and screen format. Because the corpora differ in platform ecology, model generation, period, and corpus construction as well as in modality, these differences are described rather than causally attributed, and the format result is the most interface-sensitive of them. Artist-style imitation loses its earlier prominence, a decline that survives the coding reliability checks, while everyday action and scene description forms the largest family in the adjudicated solution, a position that is sensitive to those checks. Discussion Prompting practice moved from selecting aesthetic styles toward specifying how a scene moves and how it is framed, and the prompting grammar observed here appears bound to the modality and the period. The terms that organized image prompts did not carry over intact to video prompts. These patterns suggest that the symbolic interface of human-AI co-creation is not a fixed grammar but an adaptive arrangement that responds to the salient capabilities of a generative system. The study contributes a comparative account of how the division of creative labor is reconfigured across media modalities, with implications for co-creation theory, generative interface design, and media literacy education.

items.title: Futures-Thinking for Reimagining Schools
items.abstract: Over the past century, public education has used the “factory model” to prepare students, a mindset that originates from Industrial Revolution-era reforms. Recent reform movements, such as No Child Left Behind, sought to optimize the factory model without considering new directions. This chapter introduces the concept of reimagining, rather than reforming, our schools. Reimagining education allows for dramatic changes in the structure of public education. The future needs of today’s students are dramatically different to what they were when the factory model of schooling emerged. To respond to student needs, educational leaders must develop futures-literate leadership skills. Futures-literate leaders accept and embrace change, regardless of inherent uncertainty (i.e., the emergence of generative AI technology). This chapter assists the reader by reflecting on the importance of reimagining schools, the reader’s preparedness to lead with a futures-literate mindset, and identifying areas for growth in reimagining.

items.title: Gender Difference in Trust, Vulnerability, and Emotional Attachment in Human–AI Interactions
items.abstract: As artificial intelligence (AI) gains an increasing role in the way people form emotional bonds with technology, this work specifically explores the gendered aspects of trust, vulnerability, and emotional bonding in human-AI relationships among a sample of students in a higher education environment. A cross-sectional quantitative study was conducted on 210 undergraduate and postgraduate students in the Vellore district, Tamil Nadu, India, using convenience sampling method. The results showed that gender was found to be a strong but inconsistent predictor of the behaviors in AI interactions and there were no significant differences in trust and emotional attachment. Age and field of study also had no significant effects. Students generally reported moderate levels of trust and attachment, which suggests a cautious, optimistic approach toward Artificial Intelligence. This study highlights gender as an important factor in disclosure behavior while broader demographic factors remain less influential.

items.title: Generative AI and student motivation: an SDT-guided systematic review of learning activities, motivational regulation, and measurement
items.abstract: The application of Generative AI is reshaping students’ learning. However, student motivation in GenAI-supported learning is complex and influenced by multiple factors. To fully realize the educational potential of GenAI, a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between student motivation and GenAI is necessary. To address this gap, this study conducted a systematic literature review. From the perspective of Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this review examined 39 articles published between 2023 and 2025, drawn from two databases: Web of Science and Scopus. This study provides three major findings. First, competence-related learning activities were the most frequently identified across the reviewed studies. Second, four categories were reported in relation to student motivation: GenAI characteristics, learner factors, psychological factors, and environmental factors. Third, three major aspects of motivational conceptualization are basic psychological needs, motivation construct, and motivation-related construct. In addition, quantitative questionnaires were the dominant approach used to measure these constructs. Finally, the relationship among these three findings is illustrated. The findings provide insights into student motivation in GenAI-supported learning and highlight the relevance of GenAI characteristics, learners, and the learning environment. This study also provides theoretical and practical implications for facilitating students’ motivation in GenAI-supported learning environments.

items.title: Generative AI as a bounded elicitation and evidence-synthesis layer for pain assessment in older adults with cognitive impairment
items.abstract: Pain assessment in older adults with cognitive impairment remains challenging, particularly when changes in communication make self-report difficult. Validated observational tools, caregiver and staff knowledge, clinical examination, and repeated within-person assessment remain the foundation of care. However, information from these sources may be incomplete, conflicting, or documented across different settings. Generative artificial intelligence (AI), including large language models, may help clinicians organize and review this information, but it should not independently detect, diagnose, or determine treatment for pain. In this Perspective article, we propose a person-centered, clinician-governed framework for the bounded use of generative AI in pain assessment. The framework organizes seven testable use cases under three core functions: capacity-sensitive elicitation, source-attributed synthesis, and longitudinal support and communication. Potential applications include adaptive pain interviews, identification of possible pain-related information in everyday language, structuring of behavioral observations, multi-informant synthesis, synthesis of validated nonverbal indicators, longitudinal pain-related diaries, and caregiver communication support. Each application requires clear limits, source identification, communication of uncertainty, consideration of alternative causes of distress, and mandatory clinician verification before clinical action or documentation. We also examine risks related to suggestibility, bias, medication effects, privacy, alert fatigue, workload, and overreliance on AI-generated outputs. A five-step research pathway is proposed that includes co-design, technical testing, clinical validation, evaluation across populations and care settings, and risk-based governance. Generative AI should be adopted only if prospective studies demonstrate meaningful value beyond validated assessment methods and usual clinical workflows without reducing patient choice, replacing clinical judgment, or increasing workload.

items.title: GENERATIVE AI AS A SYMPTOM OF THE POLYCRISIS OF US DIGITAL CAPITALISM AND OF THE TRUMPIAN END-TIMES FASCISM
items.abstract: The article critically interrogates why the build-out of generative “AI” in the ideological-material form it has taken in the USA can be viewed as symptomatic of the intensifying polycrisis of US digital capitalism and the US-led neo-imperial order. Employing a neo-Luddite-Marxist approach to analyse the technology of GenAI, first the eugenic-eschatological ideological underpinnings of it are examined, along with the central problematic, ecologically unsustainable technical characteristic of its development and functioning and the politico-economic conditions of its possibility which make it a symptom of the polycrisis. The second focus is the centrality of GenAI in digital capitalism’s mutation to become an even more speculative, unsustainable, environment- and society-destructive, power-centralising and worker-exploiting form – ‘Muskism’, that is parasitically dependent on the US state. Finally, it tackles the role of GenAI in the implementation of the end-times fascist project of the second Trump Administration and its deliberate escalation of the polycrisis. Keywords: AI, end-times fascism, digital capitalism, Muskism, Trump, polycrisis.

items.title: Generative AI in Intelligent Tutoring Systems: A Systematic Literature Review of Pedagogical Feedback, Conversational Interaction, and Learning Safety
items.abstract: Intelligent Tutoring Systems (ITSs) have advanced from rule-based learning environments to adaptive systems that use artificial intelligence techniques, modelling of learners and learning analytics. The wide range of systems and learning approaches makes it difficult to understand how learner data is mapped to adaptive instructional decision making. This paper reports a systematic literature review of pedagogical alignment, adaptivity, and analytics in Intelligent Tutoring Systems. This review synthesises relevant research in three inter-related dimensions of ITS design: pedagogical alignment (how tutoring strategies and learning objectives are aligned); adaptivity (how systems respond to learners' characteristics knowledge behaviour and performance); and learning analytics (how learners’ data are captured, analysed, and applied). The review mostly focuses on the integration of knowledge tracing, student modelling, educational data mining, learning analytics, and AI-based tutoring technologies in adaptive learning; it discusses the effectiveness of different adaptive learning processes; evaluation approaches; and technical and pedagogical issues related to adaptive learning (including data quality, data sparsity interpretability individualization, scalability, and model-to-pedagogy complementarity). The integration of the points of view presented in this study helps to provide a comprehensive view of the relationship between the data analyses adaptive decisions, and pedagogy used in intelligent tutoring systems. The review aims to lay a conceptual foundation for building adaptive ITSs that are more sensitive to individual learner needs, are informed by data, and are pedagogically consistent in their teaching strategies, and to suggest future research directions for the architecture of integrated adaptive ITSs in different educational settings.

items.title: Generative AI-assisted self-visualization and self-concept clarity: evidence consistent with a cognitive-mirroring mechanism in human–AI interaction
items.abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (AI) now lets people turn verbal self-descriptions into visual self-representations, creating a new setting for studying self-concept clarity (SCC) in human–AI interaction. We tested whether generative AI-assisted self-visualization (GAISV) was associated with higher short-term SCC through cognitive mirroring rather than through general immersive flow, and whether this depends on how far participants identify with the generated image. We introduce the AI Mirror Self-Integration Model and evaluated it in two stages. A pilot study (124 valid participants) examined the Cognitive Mirroring in Human-AI Self-Visualization Scale (CM-HAIS) and supported its use as a task-state measure of reflective self-processing. A randomized main experiment then recruited 328 valid participants. Primary analyses compared three conditions—GAISV, active non-self image generation, and passive image viewing ( N = 246)—with SCC measured immediately after the task and again 48–72 h later (T2 N = 216). A self-description-only condition was retained as an exploratory comparison and was not part of the primary tests. GAISV produced higher post-task and follow-up SCC than both control conditions. In parallel mediation models, the GAISV effect was primarily associated with cognitive mirroring rather than with flow, and the cognitive-mirroring indirect path was stronger than the flow path immediately after the task. Image self-identification was associated with the strength of the cognitive-mirroring path at the post-task assessment, as indicated by the index of moderated mediation; the follow-up moderation evidence was weaker. AI-generated self-images were therefore not clarifying by default. GAISV was associated with higher short-term SCC primarily when the image was experienced as personally identifying and engaged reflective cognitive mirroring rather than mere immersion. Condition differences were statistically reliable but small (Cohen’s d ≈ 0.21–0.27), and the mediation results are mechanism-consistent associations rather than evidence of causal ordering.

items.title: Generative AI, Cultural Information Risks and the Negotiation of Youth Cultural Identity: A Qualitative Comparison of University Students in Guangdong, Hong Kong and Macao
items.abstract: Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) is changing how young people access cultural knowledge and understand sociocultural narratives. Some research has examined the information risks of Generative AI (GenAI), but few have studied how young people from different cultural backgrounds perceive and are affected by these risks. Based on the interviews conducted with 33 university students in Shenzhen from Guangdong, Hong Kong and Macao, this paper conducts thematic analysis and cross-background comparison of their views on risks to cultural information, strategies for identity negotiation and related sociocultural experiences. Based on the above analysis, the three main topics are: (1) the three perceived risks: information distortion, cultural misrepresentation and information homogenization; (2) the three identity negotiation strategies in response to AI-generated cultural information: identity affirmation, identity reconsideration and identity defense; and (3) associations of language use, platform exposure and cross-regional cultural experiences with different interpretations and responses to cultural information by participants. Based on the data in this paper, it has been determined that participants' previous cultural experiences are incorporated into their perception and response of AI-generated cultural materials; therefore, this study will provide specific evidence to help improve the critical evaluation of cultural information and digital literacy education for young people in the Greater Bay Area.

items.title: Generative Artificial Intelligence as a Digital Social Mediator
items.abstract: The emergence of generative artificial intelligence and large language models has dramatically altered the landscape of digital communications. Although these new tools have made possible significant improvements in language generation and understanding, they have also increased the scalability, customization, and contextual sophistication of cyberbullying. Modern cyberbullying has also evolved from being merely a matter of using language that is hurtful and insulting to the use of computer automation and language-generation capabilities on the internet. Cyber-bullying cannot be categorized under a simplistic classification scheme but has to be envisioned as an interactional, dynamic, socio-cognitive process entailing implicit intentionality, emotions, and escalation mechanisms. Challenged by the limitations of reactive, punitive systems, this chapter unfolds the paradigm shift to generative empathic moderation (GEM), with AI performing an active virtual mediation role. Bringing together generative models, explainable AI, and human oversight, GEM seeks to diffuse toxic interactions and induce de-escalation while ensuring the reconciliation of operational optimality, responsibility, and social acceptability.

items.title: Generative Invitation: A Relational Mechanism of Heterogeneous Co-Creation
items.abstract: This paper develops generative invitation as a provisional description of relational praxis in which an addressed offering enters another participant’s historically situated activity. It distinguishes affordances, offerings, recipient uptake, counterproposal, immediate achievement, and possible changes in effective opportunities or enduring capacities. Buber, Levinas, Ricœur, Arendt, ecological affordance theory, educational scaffolding, participatory sense-making, and literary reception provide substantial philosophical precedents. The generative-relational (GR) proposal is therefore evaluated for its incremental usefulness in tracing the relation between an offering, heterogeneous receiving conditions, subsequent trajectories, and control over enabling resources. Constructed cases from aesthetics, education, interspecies encounters, and human–AI interaction illustrate both this possible scope and the differing evidence required for claims about experience, autonomy, and agency. A comparative account tests whether established theories already explain the same observations, and distinguishes productive influence from ethical legitimacy or entitlement to resulting value. Conceptual discrimination, explanatory adequacy, and normative accountability provide three separate tests of this account. Its immediate contribution is a set of revisable distinctions; whether they jointly identify an explanatory mechanism beyond existing theories remains a question for comparative and empirical inquiry.

items.title: Genetic Polymorphisms in Inflammatory Diseases: From Genetic Mechanisms to Precision Medicine
items.abstract: Inflammation is a complex biological defense response to infection, tissue injury, and other danger signals, playing a fundamental role in maintaining tissue homeostasis and immune balance. A well-regulated and transient inflammatory response facilitates pathogen clearance, limits tissue damage, and promotes tissue repair. However, when inflammatory responses become persistent, dysregulated, or fail to resolve appropriately, they may progress to chronic inflammation, thereby contributing to the initiation and progression of numerous major diseases, including autoimmune disorders, metabolic diseases, cardiovascular diseases, and cancer. Chronic inflammation is not merely characterized by sustained elevation of inflammatory mediators; rather, it represents a complex systemic process involving immune cell reprogramming, disruption of tissue barrier integrity, aberrant tissue repair, metabolic reprogramming, and remodeling of the tissue microenvironment. Accumulating evidence from genetic studies has demonstrated that inter-individual variability in the magnitude of inflammatory responses and susceptibility to inflammatory diseases is, at least in part, attributable to genetic variation within the human genome. Genetic polymorphisms encompass single nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs), insertion/deletion variants (InDels), copy number variations (CNVs), and more complex structural variants. These genetic variants can influence inflammatory responses at multiple levels by modulating gene expression, RNA processing, protein structure and function, antigen presentation, intracellular signal transduction, and immune cell function, thereby shaping individual sensitivity and responsiveness to inflammatory stimuli. Among the numerous genetic loci implicated in inflammatory diseases, the human leukocyte antigen (HLA) region, cytokine-encoding genes, pattern recognition receptor (PRR) genes, inflammasome-associated genes, and genes involved in downstream inflammatory signaling pathways have emerged as major focuses of research in the field of inflammation genetics. This chapter is organized around the framework of “genetic variation–molecular mechanisms–cellular phenotypes–disease phenotypes–clinical translation” and systematically reviews the major types of inflammation-associated genetic polymorphisms, their molecular mechanisms, and their contributions to the pathogenesis of inflammatory diseases, including rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, inflammatory bowel disease, and asthma. Furthermore, recent advances in genome-wide association studies (GWAS), fine mapping, expression quantitative trait locus (eQTL) and protein quantitative trait locus (pQTL) analyses, single-cell and spatial multi-omics, functional genomics, genome editing, and artificial intelligence are discussed to illustrate how genetic discoveries are being translated into disease risk prediction, molecular stratification, prognostic assessment, pharmacogenomics, and precision therapeutics. It is important to recognize that most complex inflammatory diseases arise from the interplay of multiple genetic factors, environmental exposures, and substantial population heterogeneity. Consequently, genetic associations do not necessarily imply causality, and genetic risk markers identified in research settings should not be interpreted as clinically validated biomarkers that are ready for routine clinical decision-making. With the continued development of multi-omics technologies, single-cell and spatial omics, and artificial intelligence, the field of inflammation genetics is evolving beyond the identification of susceptibility loci toward a deeper understanding of disease mechanisms and the realization of precision medicine.

items.title: Geographic Information Systems for Urban and Town Planning: Applications, Analytical Approaches, Challenges and Future Perspectives
items.abstract: Geographic Information Systems (GIS) have evolved from digital mapping and spatial data management tools into analytical and decision-support environments for contemporary town planning. This review critically synthesizes 20 studies covering GIS applications in urban growth modelling, land-use planning, site suitability, transportation and accessibility, infrastructure planning, environmental management, disaster-risk assessment, development control, public participation, and integration with remote sensing, BIM, artificial intelligence and emerging digital technologies. The reviewed evidence indicates that the principal value of GIS in town planning lies in its ability to integrate heterogeneous spatial and attribute datasets, perform multi-criteria and network-based analysis, represent spatial relationships, visualize alternative development scenarios, and support monitoring and decision-making. However, the literature also shows recurring limitations associated with data quality, temporal updating, interoperability, model calibration and validation, technical capacity, institutional coordination, cost, privacy and unequal access to spatial information. A cross-study synthesis is used to organize GIS applications according to planning function, analytical method, decision stage and technology integration. The review identifies a transition from GIS as a mapping and inventory system toward an integrated planning-support ecosystem combining GIS with remote sensing, BIM, IoT, cloud platforms, 3D visualization and AI/ML. Based on the synthesis, a conceptual GIS-enabled town-planning framework is proposed, linking data acquisition and quality assurance with spatial analysis, scenario modelling, stakeholder participation, decision support and continuous monitoring. The review concludes that future research should prioritize interoperable and continuously updated spatial infrastructures, transparent multi-criteria modelling, validated predictive approaches, human-centred participatory interfaces and integrated GIS–RS–BIM–AI environments.

items.title: Governing the hybrid writer: ethics-washing discourse and algorithmic governmentality in academic AI platforms
items.abstract: This study critically examines the ethical frameworks of leading generative AI platforms to understand how they discursively position student writing, construct normative subjects, and redistribute epistemic authority in higher education. By asking what kind of “ethical academic subject” these documents construct and what functions their governance discourses perform, we conducted a critical discourse analysis of publicly available ethical and governance documents from nine widely used AI platforms and one contextual state-regulatory text, using versions retrieved on 1 October 2026. Guided by three research questions, the analysis drew on an integrated framework of posthumanism, sociomateriality, Foucauldian governmentality, and ethics of care, operationalised through Fairclough's three-dimensional model. The analysis reveals how these frameworks discursively construct students as hybrid cognitive agents simultaneously empowered by augmentation and disciplined by algorithmic oversight. We identify six interlocking discursive formations: safety governance, academic integrity regulation, transparency as an epistemic virtue, human-machine augmentation, platform procedural accountability, and relational responsibility, which function not as neutral ethical guides but as a powerful layer of discursively constituted algorithmic governmentality. We argue that platform ethics is discursively positioned to reshape academic authorship and to conduct student behaviour through regimes of corporate and state-aligned governance. The asymmetry between aspirational corporate commitments and directive user obligations is consistent with what the literature terms “ethics-washing”: ethical vocabulary that performs legitimacy while preserving corporate discretion. We identify this as a discursive function, not a demonstrated corporate motive. We also suggest, as a theoretical proposition for future empirical testing, that such regimes may leave limited spaces for tactical student agency. By conceptualising platform policies as claims to educational governing authority, we expose the tensions between empowerment and control embedded in AI-mediated writing and argue for critical platform literacy as an essential response to this parallel governance regime.

items.title: Greening GenAI: sustainable solutions for higher education
items.abstract: Higher education institutions increasingly embrace and regulate Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI). While the cognitive, social, and ethical implications of GenAI are widely discussed in the current scientific discourse, the environmental disruption caused by large-scale GenAI use has remained largely ignored. As GenAI becomes integral to research and education, addressing its environmental impacts has become an increasingly urgent priority. In this Perspective, we argue that mitigating the environmental impact of GenAI requires more than advances in hardware and software efficiency; it also demands a stronger focus on user behavior as a key lever for reducing GenAI’s disruptive environmental impacts. This is particularly important given that every second, millions of prompts are submitted to GenAI systems in support of human learning, research, and knowledge acquisition. Optimizing how users interact with these systems offers scalable behavior-based strategies with the potential to substantially reduce their environmental impacts while requiring relatively modest changes in practice. We present a set of measures to promote the sustainable use of GenAI in higher education and scientific research.

items.abstract: This study investigates the effectiveness of Artificial Intelligence (AI) as a pedagogical tool to address the challenge of engaging secondary students. We explore how an AI music composing application can transform 11th grade Tamil memory poems into musical mnemonics and measure its impact against traditional methods. Grounded in Cognitive Theory of Multimedia Learning and Gardner's Theory of Multiple Intelligences, This study involved a control group that engaged in traditional reading. The experimental groups listened to the poem set to music: Rendition composed by a human, and three distinct versions (Rap, Carnatic, and Melody) generated by an AI music application. A one-way ANOVA indicated significant differences in memory scores across groups (F(4,207=25.48, p,0.001). AI-generated content performed comparably to human-composed material, with AI-Rap exhibiting the highest effectiveness. These findings confirm the efficacy and scalability of AI audio creation tools in enhancing literature education.

items.title: Health-related quality of life and marine-related health risks in coastal communities of Palawan, Philippines
items.abstract: Coastal fishing communities depend on marine resources yet face significant occupational and environmental health risks. This study asssessed health-related quality of life (HRQoL) and self-reported accidents and health outcomes among adults in three coastal municipalities of Palawan, Philippines. A cross-sectional survey recruited 431 adults across 10 barangays, with 401 complete responses analyzed. The HRQoL was assessed using the Philippine Short Form-12 (SF-12), producing Physical Component Summary (PCS-12) and Mental Component Summary (MCS-12) scores. Fifteen self-reported health items were examined using exploratory factor analysis, identifying three domains: marine accidents, musculoskeletal complaints, and infections and skin diseases. Women had higher odds of reporting marine-related accidents compared thaan men (OR = 2.07; 95% CI: 1.87–2.54). More than half of respondents (56.9%, n = 228) had PCS-12 ≤50 (mean 48.3 ± 5.7), indicating poor physical health, while 26.4% (n = 106) scored MCS-12 ≤42 (mean 47.3 ± 8.3), suggesting possible mental health concerns. Musculoskeletal complaints were the most prevalent health outcome, affecting up to 71.1% of respondents, while those in the poorest marine-based income bracket had nearly twice the odds of reporting infections and skin diseases (OR = 1.87; 95% CI: 1.22–3.86). The HRQoL varied by study site, gender, age, and education, whereas ethnicity, religion, and coastal proximity were not significantly associated. These findings showed that women and low-income fishers face greater occupational and environmental health risks. Interventions should prioritize gender-responsive safety, ergonomic support, accessible healthcare, and stronger social protection. Further qualitative research is needed to clarify the pathways that drive these disparities.

items.title: How Can Game-Theoretic Models Explain Optimal Move Selection in Mid-Game Scenarios Under Uncertainty?
items.abstract: The objective of this research paper is to study how game-theoretical models help in determining the optimal decision in a mid-game situation where there is uncertainty, high complexity related to strategies, and a large number of options available for making a decision. The paper discusses the basic ideas such as normal form and extensive form games, Nash equilibrium, subgame perfect equilibrium, Bayesian games, stochastic games, and mixed strategies that one should use when making decisions when there is insufficient information available. Specifically, the paper analyzes the methods of Bayesian belief updating, stochastic state transitions, heuristic search, Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) method, and reinforcement learning, the idea of which is to allow the identification of best decisions in cases when the computation of equilibrium is very difficult. The authors examine the examples referring to different games such as chess, poker, go, and real-time strategy games and show how game-theoretical concepts can be combined with computational solutions. The discussion brings up a significant number of drawbacks such as computational complexity, lack of full information, bounded rationality, incorrect models, and dependence on data quality. In this paper, the authors conclude that the integration of game theory with simulation and artificial intelligence provides a practical framework for developing robust and near-optimal strategies in complex uncertain environments.
